problem_data.story:
I am a Probability Field
By SOPHIA WEST

When I got back from the research institute, I was not so much exhausted as mentally drained, but the effect is similar. I let myself into the apartment in Eastwood Village, which had an absent-partner look, and took a cold shower. The present temperature according to the weather app was thirty-two degrees Celsius, but according to my thermometer, it was thirty-eight. I got dressed and went into the living room, and wished ardently that my partner Hassan were here to tell me why the whole place looked so desolate.

What do they do, I asked myself, that I have left undone? I've cleaned the floors, I've organized the books and I've straightened the cushions.... Ah! The coffee mugs. I washed them and put them back, but still the place looked partner-deserted.

It had been a difficult day; I had forgotten to charge my alarm, so I'd had to rush to make a theoretical modeling presentation at one of the quantum computing labs I consult for. My paper concerned the mathematics of systems existing in multiple simultaneous states—the probability distributions that collapse upon observation. I didn't notice the impending storm and had no umbrella when I reached the sidewalk, to find myself confronted with an almost tropical downpour. I would have turned back, but a rideshare pulled up and a woman got out, so I dashed through the rain and got in.

"University District, the Quantum Sciences Building," I said.

"Right," said the driver, and I heard the engine sputter, and then go on sputtering. After some futile attempts, she turned to me. "Sorry. You'll have to find another ride. Good luck."

If possible, it was raining still harder. I opened my bag over my head and ran for the metro: three blocks. Traffic held me up at each crossing and I was soaked when I reached the platform, just in time to miss the express. After an abnormal delay, I got one which exactly missed the connection at Central Station. The same thing happened at both ends of the cross-district line, but I found the rain had stopped when I got out at University Square.

As I walked toward the building, I passed a large construction site where they were preparing to build a new green infrastructure project—part of the city's environmental justice initiative. There was the usual crowd of observers watching the excavation machines and, in particular, a worker with a jackhammer who was breaking up some compressed sediment. While I looked, a large chunk of it fell away, and for an instant I was able to see something that looked like a piece of crystalline material, the size of a storage container. It glittered brilliantly in the sunlight, and then the chattering jackhammer hit it.

There was a faint crack and the thing disintegrated. It knocked the worker backwards, but he got right up and I realized he was not hurt. At the moment of the fracture—if so minor a thing can be called one—I felt something sting my cheek and, on touching it, found blood on my hand. I dabbed at it with a tissue but, though slight, the bleeding would not stop, so I went into a pharmacy and bought some adhesive strips which I put on the tiny cut. When I got to the lab, I found that I had missed the presentation slot.

During the day, by actual count, I heard the phrase "Let's workshop that" nine times, and another academic favorite, "The entire theoretical framework," eleven times. However, my theoretical model had been accepted without revision because nobody had noticed my absence from the presentation room. There you have what is known as the Academic World, the research game, or the grant-writing racket, depending upon which level of the hierarchy you have achieved.

The metro gave a repeat performance going home, and as I got to the apartment complex in Eastwood Village, the building manager was standing there talking to the maintenance supervisor.

She said, "Hello, Dr. West. I guess you must have just missed it at your building. We just heard a little while ago: all four elevators in the Quantum Sciences Building jammed at the same time. Sounds impossible. I guess you just missed it."

Anything can happen in academia, I thought. "That's right, I just missed it," I said, and went on in.

Behavioral economics tells us that some people are risk-seeking; I, on the other hand, seemed recently to be coincidence-prone, anomaly-adjacent, and except for the dead alarm, I'd had no control over what had been going on.

I went into our small kitchen to make a drink and reread the instructions Hassan had left, telling me how to manage by myself until he got back from his conference in Crestwood Village, a matter of ten days. How to use the coffee maker, how to operate the food processor, whom to call if I needed help. My partner used to be a professional chef and he is quite convinced that I cannot feed myself without him. He is right, but not for the reasons he supposes.

I opened the refrigerator to get some ice and saw another note: "When you take out the Juice or Cheese, Put it Right Back. And Close the Door, too."

Intimidated, I took my drink into the living room and sat down in front of the computer. As I stared at the research paper that was to establish my reputation beyond quantum computing, I noticed an error and picked up a stylus. When I put it down, it rolled off the desk, and with my eyes on the manuscript, I groped under the chair for it. Then I looked down. The stylus was standing on its end.

There, I thought to myself, is that one chance in a million we hear about, and picked up the stylus. I turned back to my paper and drank some of the cocktail in hopes of inspiration and relief from the muggy heat, but nothing came. I went back and read the whole section to try to get forward momentum, but came to a dead stop at the last sentence.

Damn the heat, damn the stylus, damn academia and grant applications. My drink was gone and I went back to the kitchen and read Hassan's notes again to see if they would be like a message from him. I noticed one that I had missed, pinned to the recycling bin: "Pickup at 6:30 AM so the idea is to Put it Here the Night Before. I love you." What can you do when he loves you?

I made another drink and went and stared out of the living room window at the courtyard opposite. The sun was out again and a woman with a remote was operating her collection of drones. They flew in formation, hoping to be allowed to land, but were not allowed to.

Drones fly as a rule in coordinated patterns and turn simultaneously, so that their solar panels all catch the sunlight at the same time. I was thinking about this elegant fact when I saw that as they were making a turn, they seemed to bunch up together. By some curious chance, they all wanted the same position in the airspace to turn in, and several collided and fell.

The woman was as surprised as I and went to one of the damaged drones and picked it up. She stood there shaking her head from side to side, examining its rotors.

My speculations about this peculiar aerial traffic accident were interrupted by loud voices in the hallway. Since our building is usually very well behaved, I was astonished to hear what sounded like an incipient argument, and among the angry voices I recognized that of my neighbor, Felix, a very quiet guy who works in media production and has never, to my knowledge, caused disturbances, particularly in the late afternoon.

"You can't accuse me of that!" I heard him shout. "I tell you I bought this deck this afternoon and it wasn't opened till we started to play!"

Several other loud voices started at the same time.

"Nobody gets five royal flushes in a row!"

"Yeah, and only when you were dealer!"

The tone of the argument was beginning to get ugly, and I opened the door to offer Felix help if he needed it. There were four people confronting him, evidently torn between the desire to make an angry exit and the impulse to stay and confront him further. His face was furiously red and he looked stunned.

"Here!" he said, holding out a deck of cards, "For heaven's sake, examine them yourselves if you think they're marked!"

The nearest person struck them up from his hand. "Okay, magician! So they're not marked! All I know is five royal...."

His voice trailed away. He and the others stared at the scattered cards on the floor. About half were face down, as might be expected, and the rest face up—all spades.

Someone must have called for it, because at that moment the elevator arrived and the four people, with half frightened, incredulous looks, and in silence, got in and were taken down. My friend stood looking at the neatly arranged cards.

"Unbelievable!" he said, and started to pick them up. "My God, what a session...."

I helped him and said to come in for a drink and tell me all about it, but I had an idea what I would hear.

After a while, he calmed down, but he still seemed dazed.

"Never seen anything to equal it," he said. "Wouldn't have believed it. Those people didn't believe it. Every round normal, nothing unusual about the hands—three of a kind, a low straight, that sort of thing and one person got queens over tens, until it gets to be my deal. Brother! Royal flush—every time! And each time, somebody else has four aces...."

He started to perspire again, so I got up to fix him another drink. There was one bottle of tonic water left, but when I tried to open it, the cap broke and glass fragments got into the bottle.

"I'll have to go down for more tonic," I said.

"I'll come, too. I need air."

At the convenience store on the corner, the clerk gave me three bottles in what must have been a weak bag, because as he handed them to me over the counter, the bottom gave and they fell onto the tile floor. None of them broke, although the fall must have been from at least five feet. Felix was too absorbed in his thoughts to notice and I was getting used to anomalies. We left the proprietor with his mouth open and met the building manager, looking in at the door, also with her mouth open.

On the sidewalk, a man walking in front of Felix stopped suddenly to check his phone and Felix, to avoid bumping him, stepped into the bike lane and a cyclist swerved to avoid Felix. The pavement was still wet and the cyclist skidded, their rear wheel lightly tapping the front of one of those small electric scooters, which was going rather fast. It turned sideways and, without any side-slip, went right up the steps of a building opposite, coming to rest with its front wheel inside the entrance, which a woman opened at that moment.

The sight of this threw another cyclist into a skid, and when she and the first cyclist had stopped sliding around, they were positioned face to face, arranged crosswise to the bike lane. This gave them exactly no room to move either forward or backward, for one bike had its back to a bench and the other to a lamppost.

Although rather wide, this is a two-way bike lane, and in no time at all, traffic was backed up from both directions as far as the intersections. Everyone was ringing their bell.

The building manager was frustrated—more so when she tried to put through a call to the maintenance office from the panel in the lobby.

It was malfunctioning.

Upstairs, the wind was blowing into the apartment and I closed the windows, mainly to shut out the commotion and the noise. Felix had brightened up considerably.

"I'll stay for one more drink and then I'm due at the studio," he said. "You know, I think this would make content for our channel." He grinned and nodded toward the chaos.

When he was gone, I noticed it was getting dark and turned on the desk lamp. Then I saw the window blinds. They were all twisted in spirals, except one. That was twisted in three spirals.

All right, I told myself, it was the wind. But I felt the time had come for me to get expert advice, so I went to the phone to call Ruth. Ruth is an associate professor of theoretical physics at a university uptown and lives near us. She had collaborated with me years ago on a paper about particle correlations across distances—what Einstein famously called "spooky action"—and I trusted her judgment on strange phenomena. She is highly analytical, but we believe she knows everything.

When I picked up the receiver, the line sounded dead and I thought, more trouble. Then I heard someone cough and I said hello. Ruth's voice said, "Sophia? You must have picked up the receiver just as we were connected. That's a remarkably unlikely coincidence."

"Not in the least," I said. "Come on over here. I've got something for you to analyze."

"Well, as a matter of fact, I was calling to ask you and Hassan—"

"Hassan's away for the week. Can you get over here quickly? It's urgent."

"Immediately," she said, and hung up.

While I waited, I thought I might try working on a few paragraphs of my research paper—perhaps something would come now. It did, and I was making progress on my introduction about probability states and their coexistence before measurement. I came to a point where I needed to describe this central phenomenon in technical terms for my quantum-literate audience. The word I needed began with the letters S-U-P-E-R, but I hesitated, wondering if it was too technical for the introduction. I stopped at the letter P and looked at what I had typed. I had unaccountably hit all five keys one step to the side of the correct ones. A row of gibberish stared back at me. With my face flushed, I deleted the line.

This was absolutely not my day.

"Well," Ruth said, "nothing you've told me is impossible or supernatural. Just very, very improbable. In fact, the odds against that card game alone would lead me to suspect Felix, well as I know him. It's all those other things...."

She got up and walked over to the window and looked at the hot twilight while I waited. Then she turned around; she had a look of concern.

"Sophia, you're a rational person, so I don't think you'll take offense at what I'm going to say. What you have told me is so impossibly unlikely, and the odds against it so astronomical, that I must consider the possibility that you're either fabricating this or you're experiencing a perceptual anomaly." I started to get up and protest, but she motioned me back. "I know, but don't you see that that is far more likely than...." She stopped and shook her head. Then she brightened. "I have an idea. Maybe we can have a demonstration."

She thought for a tense minute and snapped her fingers. "Have you any coins on you?"

"Why, yes," I said. "Quite a few." I reached into my pocket. There must have been nearly three dollars in various denominations. "Do you think they'll each have the same date, perhaps?"

"Did you accumulate all those coins today?"

"No. During the week."

She shook her head. "In that case, no. Discounting the fact that you could have arranged it, if my preliminary theory is correct, that would be actually impossible. It would involve temporal reversal. I'll tell you about it later. No, just throw down the coins. Let's see if they all come up heads."

I moved away from the carpet and tossed the handful of coins onto the floor. They clattered and bounced—and bounced together—and stacked themselves into a neat pile.

I looked at Ruth. Her eyes were narrowed. Without a word, she took a handful of coins from her own pocket and threw them.

These coins didn't stack. They just fell into an exactly straight line, the adjacent ones touching.

"Well," I said, "what more do you need?"

"Good grief," she said, and sat down. "I suppose you know that there are two great apparently opposite principles governing the Universe—entropy and negentropy. Random distribution on the beach is an example of entropy and living systems are examples of negentropy. The motions of particles in a gas are what we call random, but there are so many of them, we treat them statistically and derive thermodynamic laws—quite reliable. It isn't theoretically absolute; it's just a matter of extreme probability. Now living systems, on the other hand, seem not to depend on probability at all; actually, they work against it. Or you might say they are certainly not accidental manifestations."

"Do you mean," I asked in some confusion, "that some form of life is controlling the coins and—the other things?"

She shook her head. "No. All I mean is that improbable events usually have improbable explanations. When I see a statistical law being violated, I don't say to myself, 'Here's a miracle.' I revise my understanding of the principles. Something—I don't know what—is happening, and it seems to involve probability, and it seems to center around you. Were you still in that building when the elevators stuck? Or near it?"

"I guess I must have been. It happened just after I left."

"Hm. You're the epicenter, all right. But why?"

"Epicenter of what?" I asked. "I feel as though I were the epicenter of a probability storm. Something has it in for me!"

Ruth grinned. "Don't be superstitious. And especially don't anthropomorphize."

"Well, if it's the opposite of entropy, it's got to be a living system."

"On what basis? All we know for certain is that random events are being reorganized. A crystal, for example, is not alive, but it's a non-random arrangement of particles.... I wonder." She had a faraway, contemplative look.

I was beginning to feel hungry and the drinks had worn off.

"Let's go out and eat," I said. "There's not a thing in the kitchen and I'm not allowed to cook. Only eggs and coffee."

We put on our jackets and went down to the street. From either end, we could hear tow trucks removing the stalled vehicles. There were, by this time, a number of harassed traffic officers directing the maneuver and we heard one of them say to the building manager, "I don't know what's going on around here. Every single vehicle's got something wrong with it. They can't any of them back out for one reason or another. Never seen anything like it."

Near us, two pedestrians were doing a curious little dance as they tried to pass one another; as soon as one of them moved aside to let the other pass, the other would move to the same side. They both had embarrassed grins on their faces, but before long their grins were replaced by looks of suspicion and then determination.

"All right, wise guy!" they shouted in unison, and barged ahead, only to collide. They backed off and threw simultaneous punches which met in mid-air. Then began one of the most remarkable encounters ever witnessed—a confrontation in which fist hit fist but never anything else, until both combatants backed away undefeated, muttering identical excuses and threats.

The building manager appeared at that moment. Her face was flushed. "You all right, Dr. West?" she asked. "I don't know what's happening around here, but ever since this afternoon, things are going haywire. Martinez!" she shouted—she could succeed as an auctioneer. "Bring those people over here!"

Three people in a confused tangle, with their half-open umbrellas intertwined, were brought across the street, which meant climbing over bike racks. Martinez, a competent young security officer, seemed self-conscious; the people seemed not to be.

"All right, now, Ms. Wheeler!" one of them said. "Let go of my umbrella and we'll say no more about it!"

"And so now it's Ms. Wheeler, is it?" said her adversary.

The third, a younger woman with her back turned to us, her umbrella also caught in the tangle, pulled at it tentatively, at which the other two glared at her. She turned her head away and tried to let go, but the handle was caught in her sleeve. She looked up and I saw it was Hassan. My chef-partner.

"Oh, Sophia!" he said, and managed to detach himself. "Are you all right?" Was I all right!

"Hassan! What are you doing here?"

"I was so worried, and when I saw all this, I didn't know what to think." He pointed to the stalled vehicles. "Are you really all right?"

"Of course I'm all right. But why...."

"The Crestwood Village operator said someone kept dialing and dialing the conference center and there wasn't anyone on the line, so then she had it traced and it came from our phone here. I kept calling back, but I only got a busy signal. Oh, dear, are you sure you're all right?"

I put my arm around him and glanced at Ruth. She had an inward look. Then I caught the building manager's eye. It had a thoughtful, almost suspicious cast to it.

"Trouble does seem to follow you, Dr. West," was all she said.

When we got upstairs, I turned to Ruth. "Explain to Hassan," I said. "And incidentally to me. I'm not properly informed yet."

She did so, and when she got to the summary, I had the feeling he was a step ahead of her.

"In other words, you think it's something organic?"

"Well," Ruth said, "I'm trying to think of anything else it might be. I'm not doing so well," she confessed.

"But so far as I can see," Hassan answered, "it's mere probability manipulation, without any overall pattern."

"Not quite. It has a center. Sophia is the center."

Hassan looked at me with a curious expression for a moment. "Do you feel all right, darling?" he asked me. I nodded brightly. "You'll think this silly of me," he went on to Ruth, "but could separate particles somehow be linked across distance—could that explain it? Like in our old paper?"

Ruth shook her head firmly. "That's correlation, not causation. The particles we wrote about share information instantaneously, yes, but they don't manipulate probability fields. What we're seeing here involves energy transfer and pattern formation. Very different phenomenon."

"Electromagnetic fields, then?"

"Absolutely not. For one thing, most of the objects affected weren't conductive—and don't forget electromagnetism is a force, not a form of energy itself, and a great deal of energy has been involved. I admit the energy has mainly been supplied by the objects themselves, but in an electromagnetic field, all you'd get would be stored potential energy, such as when a charged particle moves in a field. Then it would just stay there, like a capacitor. These things do a lot more than that—they continue moving."

"Why did you mention a crystal before? Why not a life-form?"

"Only an analogy," said Ruth. "A crystal resembles life in that it has a definite structure and exhibits growth, but that's all. I'll agree this—phenomenon—has no discernible structure and motion is involved, but plants don't move and amoebas have no fixed shape. Then a crystal accumulates material, but it does not transform what it accumulates; it merely rearranges it into a non-random pattern. In this case, it's rearranging random events and it has a nucleus and it seems to be growing—at least in what you might call improbability."

Hassan frowned. "Then what is it? What's it made of?"

"I should say it was made of the probability distributions themselves. Like particles existing in multiple states simultaneously until observed—except this phenomenon seems to be manipulating which states manifest. Another thing that's like a crystal is that it appears to be forming around a nucleus not of its own composition—the way a speck of dust in a supersaturated solution becomes the nucleus of crystallization."

"Sounds like the pearl in an oyster," Hassan said, and gave me an impertinent look.

"Why," I asked Ruth, "did you say the coins couldn't have the same date? I mean apart from the unlikely chance I got them that way?"

"Because I don't think this phenomenon got started before today and everything that's happened can all be described as improbable events here and now. The dates were already there, and to change them would require retroactive causation, reversing time. That's out, in my book. That telephone now—"

The doorbell rang. We were not surprised to find it was the phone technician. She took the device apart and made disapproving sounds.

"I guess you dropped it on the floor," she said with strong disapproval.

"Certainly not," I said. "Is it broken?"

"Not exactly broken, but—" She shook her head and took it apart some more.

Ruth went over and they discussed the problem in undertones. Finally the technician left and Hassan called the conference center to reassure them. Ruth tried to explain to me what had happened with the phone.

"You must have jostled something loose. And then you replaced the handset in such a way that the contact wasn't quite open."

"But for heaven's sake, Hassan says the calls were going on for a long time! I phoned you only a short time ago and it must have taken him nearly two hours to get here from Crestwood Village."

"Then you must have done it twice and the vibrations in the floor—something like that—just happened to cause the right induction patterns. Yes, I know how you feel," she said, seeing my expression. "It's beginning to intensify."

Hassan was through telephoning and suggested going out for dinner. I was so pleased to see him that I'd forgotten all about being hungry.

"I'm in no mood to cook," he said. "Let's get away from all this."

Ruth raised an eyebrow. "If all this, as you call it, will let us."

In the lobby, we ran into Felix, looking satisfied in a media way.

"I've been assigned to cover the story—who could be better?—I live here. So far, I don't quite get what's been happening. I've been talking to the building manager, but she didn't say much. I got the feeling she thinks you're involved in some mystical way. Hello, Ruth, what's with you?"

"She's got a theory," said Hassan. "Come and eat with us and she'll tell you all about it."

Since we decided on a climate-controlled restaurant nearby in the arts district, we walked. The jam of vehicles didn't seem to be any less than before and we saw the building manager again. She was talking to a city inspector, and when she caught sight of us, she said something that made the inspector look at us with interest. Particularly at me.

"If you want your umbrella, Mr. McCoy," the building manager said, "it's at the security office. What there's left of it, that is."

Hassan thanked her and there was a short pause, during which I felt the speculative regard of the inspector. I pulled out a packet of mints, which I had opened, as always, by tearing off the top. I happened to have it upside down and all the mints fell out. Before I could move my foot to obscure what they had spelled out on the sidewalk, the two officials saw it. The inspector gave me a hard look, but said nothing. I quickly kicked the insulting mints into the gutter.

When we got to the restaurant, it was crowded but cool—although it didn't stay cool for long. We sat down at a side table near the entrance and ordered gin and tonics as we looked at the menu. Sitting at the next table were a large woman, wearing a very elaborate, brilliant purple evening gown, and a thin, sour-looking man in formal wear. When the server returned, they preempted him and began ordering dinner fussily: a salad for the man, and gazpacho, crab cakes and chocolate mousse for the large woman.

I tasted my drink. It was most peculiar; salt seemed to have been used instead of sugar. I mentioned this and my companions tried theirs, and made faces.

The server was concerned and apologetic, and took the drinks back to the bar across the room. The bartender looked over at us and tasted one of the drinks. Then he dumped them in his sink with a puzzled expression and made a new batch. After mixing this, he set out a row of glasses, put ice in them and began to pour.

That is to say he tilted the shaker over the first one, but nothing came out. He tapped it against the side of the bar and tried again. Still nothing. Then he took off the top and probed into it with his stirrer, his face pink with frustration.

I had the impression that the shaker had frozen solid. Well, ice is a crystal, I thought to myself.

The other bartender gave him a fresh shaker, but the same thing happened, and I saw no more because the customers sitting at the bar crowded around in front of him, offering suggestions. Our server came back, baffled, saying he'd have the drinks in a moment, and went to the kitchen. When he returned, he had the woman's gazpacho and some bread, which he put down, and then went to the bar, where the audience had grown larger.

Hassan lit a cigarette and said, "I suppose this is all part of it, Sophia. Incidentally, it seems to be getting warmer in here."

It was, and I had the feeling the place was quieter—a background noise had stopped. It dawned on me that I no longer heard the faint hum of the air-conditioner over the entrance, and as I started to say so, I made a gesture toward it. My hand collided with Hassan's when he tapped his cigarette over the ashtray, and the cigarette landed in the neighboring gazpacho.

"Hey! What's the idea?" snarled the sour-looking man.

"I'm terribly sorry," I said. "It was an accident. I—"

"Throwing cigarettes at people!" the large woman said.

"I really didn't mean to," I began again, getting up. There must have been a loose thread in the edge of their tablecloth which one of my bracelet clasps caught on, because as I stepped out from between the closely set tables, I pulled everything—tablecloth, silverware, water glasses, salt and pepper shakers and the gazpacho-à-la-nicotine—onto the floor.

The large woman surged from the booth and slapped me forcefully. The man raised his fists and postured as boxers are popularly supposed to do. The owner of the place, a woman with distinctive silver hair, hustled toward us with a determined manner. I tried to explain what had happened, but I was outshouted, and the owner frowned darkly.
